title: Rare forms and words that occur once

objectives.can: Analyse a rare or unique form by its stem marks, endings and root, and say how sure the analysis is.

explanation.summary: Most verbs in the Aramaic of the Bible are in the Peal, Pael, Haphel, Hithpeel or Hithpaal. A small number are in stems that occur a dozen times or only once. This lesson gives a method for such forms: read the prefix, the stem mark, the root and the ending, then say how sure the result is.

sections.heading: The rare stems and how many forms there are
body: The analysed texts hold about a thousand verb forms in the common stems and only a few dozen in the rest. The count below is the number of forms the edition labels with each stem. The Hophal and the Shaphel are the only rare stems with a dozen forms or more; the others have three forms or fewer, and four of them have a single form.

Two of the labels depend on the prefix alone. The edition calls a reflexive or passive form with the prefix הִתְ- a Hithpeel or Hithpaal, and the same stem with the prefix אִתְ- or אֶתְ- an Ithpeel or Ithpaal. The prefix differs; the stem is the same kind of stem.

sections.heading: A method for a form you do not know
body: Take the word in four steps. First remove what is not part of the verb: a prefixed וְ- or לְ-, a suffix. Then look at the front of what remains: it is the stem mark. Next find the root: the three consonants that stay in every form of the verb. Last read the ending, which gives person, gender and number, or marks a participle or infinitive.
The method is shown on the one Hithpolel. The word הִתְרוֹמַמְתָּ stands in Daniel 5:23, where Daniel says that the king 'lifted himself up' against the Lord of heaven.

the consonants רוּם, as in the noun for 'height' and the Polel participle in Daniel 4:34; the middle letter is a vowel letter

sections.heading: The Hophal and the Shaphel
body: The Hophal is the passive of the Haphel. It has a prefix ה- with a vowel of the u-class or o-class in most forms, and a passive sense: הוּסְפַת 'it was added' (Daniel 4:33), הֻעַל 'he was brought in' (Daniel 5:13), הֳקִימַת 'it was made to stand' (Daniel 7:4). Not every Hophal has such a vowel: הָתְקְנַת in Daniel 4:33 and הָנְחַת in Daniel 5:20 begin with qamets.

The Shaphel is a causative like the Haphel, but with שׁ where the Haphel has ה. In the texts it belongs to two groups of verbs. One is the verb 'deliver', which has Shaphel forms nine times, all in Daniel 3 and 6: perfect שֵׁיזִיב, participle מְשֵׁיזִב and infinitive לְשֵׁיזָבוּתֵהּ. The other is the verb 'complete', with five forms, all in Ezra: perfect שַׁכְלִילוּ and infinitive לְשַׁכְלָלָה. Ezra 6:15 adds וְשֵׁיצִיא, a Shaphel perfect of a verb that means 'bring to an end'.

The Hishtaphel is the reflexive or passive stem of the Shaphel: the imperfect יִשְׁתַּכְלְלוּן in Ezra 4:13 says of the walls that they 'will be finished'. It has both the שׁ of the Shaphel and the ת of the reflexive after the imperfect prefix.

sections.heading: Ithpeel, Ithpaal and the Polel-type stems
body: The Ithpeel forms are אִתְגְּזֶרֶת 'was cut' (Daniel 2:45), אֶתְעֲקַרָה 'were rooted up' (Daniel 7:8) and אֶתְכְּרִיַּת 'was distressed' (Daniel 7:15). Each has the prefix אִתְ- or אֶתְ- and is a perfect. The two Ithpaal forms are אִתְיָעַטוּ in Daniel 6:8 and אֶשְׁתַּנִּי in Daniel 3:19. In the second the ת of the prefix and the first root consonant ש have changed places. Grammarians describe this as a regular change when the first root consonant is a sibilant.

The Polel is the Pael-type stem of a verb whose middle root letter is a vowel letter. In Daniel 4:34 the king praises (a Pael participle), extols (the Polel participle וּמְרוֹמֵם) and honours (a Pael participle) the King of heaven. The Ithpoel אֶשְׁתּוֹמַם in Daniel 4:16 and the Hithpolel above belong to the same family of patterns.

sections.heading: How sure is the analysis?
body: A common form is learned from many examples. A rare form rests on the pattern and on one or two verses, and the analysis should be held with that in mind. Three degrees are useful. The analysis is firm when the prefix, the pattern and the ending all agree and the sentence fits (the Hophal וְהוּבַד 'and it perished' in Daniel 7:11). It is likely when the form fits but only one stem mark is clear. It is open when the form could be read in more than one way.

The Saphel is open. The edition files מְסוֹבְלִין in Ezra 6:3 under the Saphel, but the root of the verb itself begins with ס, so the form alone does not show whether this ס is a stem prefix or the first root consonant. The edition's label is one reading of a form found once.

Words that occur only once are a separate matter from rare stems. Some seventy verb headwords in the texts have a single form each: for them the meaning rests on one verse, on the context, and on related words in the Semitic languages. Read such a gloss as the best reading of that verse, not as a range of uses. The edition's analysis is hand-checked but has a few slips: always test a person or number against the subject of the sentence.

misunderstandings: A rare stem is not a different language. It is the same prefix-and-pattern system as the common stems, applied to fewer verbs.
An Ithpeel is not a mistake for a Hithpeel. The prefix is spelled אִתְ- or אֶתְ- instead of הִתְ-, and the stem is a reflexive or passive stem in the same way.
The ה of a Hophal does not make it the same as a Haphel. Look at the vowel after the prefix and at the sense: the Hophal is passive.
Do not treat the meaning of a word that occurs once as proven. It is a reading of one verse. The edition's tag for a unique form is also a reading, and should be tested against the sentence.

deeper.heading: Daniel and Ezra
body: The books use different verbs in some stems. All the Shaphel forms of the verb 'deliver' stand in Daniel, and all those of the verb 'complete' in Ezra; the form of the stem is the same, but the verbs are not shared. The Hophal is the other way round: eleven of its twelve forms are in Daniel and one is in Ezra (Ezra 4:15). A reader who learns the rare stems should therefore learn them with the verbs they appear with.

examples.analysis: The only Hithpolel in the texts: a perfect, second person masculine singular. Daniel tells the king that he lifted himself up against the Lord of heaven. The prefix is reflexive, the root has a vowel letter in the middle, and the pattern doubles the last consonant.
